newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania OSCE head did not resign for personal reasons - paper.
newsitem.headline: Albania OSCE head did not resign for personal reasons - paper.

text.p: The head of an organisation monitoring Albania's elections, who stepped down earlier this week, has denied he resigned for personal reasons, a newspaper here said on Thursday.

Daily Gazeta Shqiptare quoted Brian Pridham, head of the democracy and human rights arm here of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) as saying he quit in protest at the way the elections, due on June 29, are being handled.

"I don't want to jeopardise the work of my colleagues, but I cannot accept the official version that I had personal reasons... It's not true that I pulled out of the mission for personal reasons," Pridham quoted the newspaper as saying.
The newspaper said Pridham refused to elaborate, saying he did not want to endanger the OSCE's mission in Albania.
The paper said Pridham was still in Tirana.
The OSCE said on Tuesday Briton Pridham had resigned for personal reasons and returned to England. It denied he quit out of concerns about the way the election was being handled.

Albania is due to hold elections after spinning into anarchy following the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes earlier this year. As the election nears, tensions have been mounting and observers have voiced various concerns.

The paper said Pridham had written to ambassador Herbert Grubmayr, the representative here of the OSCE's envoy to Albania Franz Vranitzky, alleging that high-level circles in the organisation were seeking to influence the outcome of the vote.

OSCE spokesman Jeff Murray said the organisation was standing by its original statement that Pridham's resignation was for personal reasons. It came days after top officials highlighted security and practical concerns about the vote.
Murray said the OSCE in Albania understood that the basis of Pridham's resignation letter to its Warsaw-based Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) was "essentially personal".
If the letter had contained the allegations reported in the newspaper, he said, "I can categorically deny that. We do not have a political agenda here."
Observers at the poll, including the OSCE and other organisations, would total about 1,000 people.
Murray said "It would be naive not to expect irregularities and attempts at manipulation, but the monitors should be able to see these.
"There may be practical problems -- like getting the candidate list ready in time for the OSCE to print ballot papers -- but as yet there was no reason to anticipate a delay in the poll," he added.
